title: India's Economy Likely Grew 7.2% Last Quarter. It Is Still the Fastest-Growing Major Economy on Earth.
excerpt: A Reuters poll of 45 economists expects GDP growth eased from 7.8% in October-December. The data, due Friday, will be the first real measure of how tariffs and the Iran war have begun to bite.
body:
India's economic growth likely slowed in the January-March quarter, pulled down by weakening external demand and the early effects of a global trade war. It is still comfortably the fastest-growing major economy in the world.

Gross domestic product is expected to have expanded 7.2% year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026, according to the median forecast in a Reuters poll of 45 economists. That represents a deceleration from the better-than-expected 7.8% growth posted in the October-December quarter, but remains well above the 6.1% floor of the forecast range.

The data, due at 4 PM IST on Friday, June 5, will be only the second quarterly GDP print under India's revised national accounts system, after the government shifted its base year to 2022-23 from 2011-12 and updated parts of its methodology in February.

## What Drove the Slowdown

A series of external shocks converged during the quarter. Higher US tariffs on Indian goods — imposed as part of President Trump's broader trade offensive — weighed on export-oriented industries, particularly in textiles, chemicals and light manufacturing. The US-Israeli war with Iran, which began in March, drove crude oil prices sharply higher and introduced supply chain uncertainty that has persisted into the current quarter.

"Underlying drivers suggest a transition from broad-based expansion to a more uneven growth profile," said Dhiraj Nim, economist at ANZ. "Government spending likely maintained a healthy pace of growth, while external demand weakened amid global disruptions."

Government capital expenditure — which has been the primary engine of investment growth for the past three years — continued at a strong pace, partially offsetting the drag from private sector caution. Agricultural growth remained resilient, supported by a reasonable winter crop season.

## The Private Investment Gap

The GDP numbers will renew attention on India's most persistent economic challenge: the reluctance of the private sector to invest at scale. Despite robust profits and healthy balance sheets, Indian companies have been slow to commit to new capacity, leaving government capital expenditure to carry a disproportionate share of the growth burden.

Economists argue that private investment is critical for generating the well-paying jobs India needs for the millions entering its workforce each year. Without it, growth remains dependent on government spending and consumer demand — a combination that works in the short term but is difficult to sustain.

The Iran war has made the investment calculus harder. Energy-intensive industries face higher costs, export-oriented firms face uncertain markets, and the broader geopolitical environment makes long-term planning difficult.

## The Base Year Shift

The revised GDP methodology introduces a complication for historical comparisons. The shift to a 2022-23 base year and updated estimation techniques make direct quarter-on-quarter comparisons with pre-revision data imprecise.

Gross value added — a measure of economic activity that strips out taxes and subsidies and is often considered a cleaner gauge of underlying momentum — was estimated at 7.3% growth for the quarter, based on a smaller sample of forecasters.

## Looking Ahead

The real test comes in the next two quarters, when the full impact of oil above $95, the Hormuz disruption, and the escalating tariff war will show up in the data. India's growth trajectory is not in doubt — no credible forecast puts it below 6% for the full year. The question is whether the composition of growth can shift from government-led to broad-based before the external shocks exhaust the fiscal space that makes government spending possible.

For now, India's position as the world's fastest-growing major economy remains secure. But the margin of comfort is narrowing, and the data due Friday will show exactly how much.
nri_angle: For NRIs tracking India's economic trajectory, the 7.2% number is impressive by any global standard — China managed 4.7% and the US 2.3% over the same period. But a growth model dependent on government spending while private investment stays muted is one that sustains momentum for quarters, not decades. The sectors that employ diaspora talent — technology, pharmaceuticals, financial services — face specific headwinds the aggregate number obscures.
author: Diaspora Desk
